title: Municipal Communication as Relational Infrastructure for Adaptive Urban Climate Governance
content: Urban climate governance requires actor coordination, integration of distributed knowledge, and iterative revision of public action. Municipal communication is identified as relational infrastructure that can delineate climate governance, assign public responsibilities for its management, and shape conditions for acceptance or rejection of environmental policies. Its conceptualization in specialized climate action literature is asymmetrical in relation to governance, participation, and sustainability as an established core. A non-exhaustive, theoretically oriented conceptual review guided by a problematizing logic compares the treatment of communication across four academic traditions: climate and collaborative governance; participation, coproduction, and deliberation; climate change communication; and collaborative planning and interpretive approaches. A communication model for adaptive urban climate governance, conceived as an institutional configuration, is developed through mechanisms including social problem translation, institutional coordination, and legitimation. Its dimensions (integration, continuity, connectivity, reciprocity, accessibility, contestability, and linkage to decision-making) condition communicative governance capacity. The model connects mechanisms with an analytical sequence and its scope conditions, incorporating a loop of strategic orientation, interaction, implementation and participation, feedback, and learning for institutional readjustment and climate policy adaptation. The proposal enables examination of communicative configurations that may contribute to adaptive and procedurally legitimate urban climate governance, without attributing automatic effects on effectiveness to them.
